title: Linux Fundamentals I: the terminal is your best friend
description: First Linux commands: who you are, where you are, and how to navigate the filesystem without leaving the terminal.

1.title: Who am I and where am I?
1.body:
## Identity and location

Two existential questions of the terminal, answered by two commands:

```bash
whoami     # your user
pwd        # your current directory (print working directory)
```

The **prompt** gives you clues too: `usuario@host:~$` means you're in your home
(`~` is the shortcut for `/home/tu-usuario`). The `$` means a regular user; if you saw `#`,
you'd be root (careful with what you type!).

## Basic navigation

```bash
ls          # list contents
ls -l       # details: permissions, size, date
ls -la      # details + hidden files (those starting with .)
cd /etc     # go to an absolute directory
cd Documentos   # relative (from wherever you are)
cd ..       # go up one level
cd ~        # back to home
cd -        # back to the previous directory
```

Tip: the **Tab** key autocompletes names — use it mercilessly. And `Ctrl+L` clears the
screen (faster than typing `clear`).

## Standard hierarchy (FHS)

In Linux everything hangs from `/` (the root of the system, not to be confused with the root user):

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `/home` | users' personal folders |
| `/etc` | system configuration |
| `/var/log` | logs |
| `/tmp` | temporary files |
| `/usr/bin` | installed executables |

Unlike Windows, there's no `C:\`: paths use `/` and there are no drive letters.

2.title: Create, copy, move and destroy
2.body:
## The life cycle of a file

```bash
mkdir -p proyectos/ctf/notas    # create the whole branch of directories
touch informe.txt               # create it empty (or update its date if it exists)
cp informe.txt copia.txt        # copy
mv copia.txt ~/Documentos/      # move (and rename: mv a.txt b.txt!)
cat informe.txt                 # view the whole content
head -n 5 informe.txt           # first 5 lines
tail -f /var/log/syslog         # follow a log live (Ctrl+C to exit)
rm copia.txt                    # delete a file
rm -rf proyectos                # delete a directory and everything in it — NO TRASH BIN
```

`rm -rf` doesn't forgive: there's no Ctrl+Z. Read it twice before pressing Enter, especially
if it starts with `/` or contains `*`.

## Finding things

```bash
find /etc -name "*.conf"            # files by name
find / -type f -size +100M 2>/dev/null   # huge files (errors to /dev/null)
grep -i "error" app.log             # text inside files (-i ignores case)
grep -r "password" ./configuración  # recursive search
```

## Your first self-contained flag

The flag exercises in this room are solved with local tools. Decode
this in your terminal (it's Base64):

```bash
echo "RkxBR3tjb21hbmRvc19kZWxfdGlhbn0=" | base64 -d
```

The result is this task's flag. Welcome to the art of decoding :)

options.a: An error: touch only updates the dates of existing files
options.c: It opens an editor so you can write it
options.d: Nothing: touch is an alias of cat

3.title: Help, pipes and redirection
3.body:
## Nobody knows every command

```bash
man ls          # full manual (q to quit)
ls --help       # summary of options
man -k password # search the manuals by keyword (apropos)
```

## Pipes and redirection: the UNIX philosophy

Each command does ONE thing well; you compose them with `|` (pipe):

```bash
cat acceso.log | grep "401" | wc -l        # how many unauthorized accesses?
ps aux | grep nginx                        # nginx processes
history | grep ssh                         # which ssh commands have I run?
```

Output redirection:

```bash
echo "hola" > saludo.txt     # create/overwrite
echo "otra línea" >> saludo.txt   # add (append)
comando 2> errores.txt       # only stderr to a file
comando > /dev/null 2>&1     # total silence (everything into the void)
```

## Star commands for later

```bash
sort | uniq -c | sort -nr    # top repeated lines (you'll see this A LOT in CTFs)
cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd      # first column of a file delimited by :
awk '{print $1}'             # first column of whitespace-separated text
```

With navigation, files and pipes you're already dangerous in a terminal. The next
room in the module: permissions, users and processes — where privilege escalation begins.

4.title: Lab: explore the real system
4.body:
## Practice in the lab

Spin up the lab (panel above) and log in with:
```bash
docker exec -it lab-linux-explore-shell-1 su - explorer
```

### Exercise 1: hidden dotfile
```bash
ls -la ~                          # -a shows hidden files (those starting with .)
cat ~/.secret_flag                # there's the flag!
```

### Exercise 2: search system files
```bash
grep FLAG /etc/passwd             # look for the word FLAG in passwd
```

These are EXACTLY the commands you'll use on every compromised machine.
